learningObjective: Identify correct properties of differential testing (running two implementations of the same spec on many random inputs and comparing outputs) versus golden testing.
stem: Which statements about differential testing (as applied to kernel/compiler correctness) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Differential testing compares outputs of two independent implementations of the same specification on many (often randomly generated) inputs; it is especially effective at surfacing corner-case bugs (empty shapes, extreme values, unusual strides) that a single golden test might miss.

A differential-testing framework must record inputs that trigger a discrepancy so that the failure can be reproduced deterministically; without seed recording, non-deterministic failures degrade to noise and cannot be triaged.

Differential testing between an implementation and itself (e.g., torch.compile vs eager) always yields identical outputs by construction; any discrepancy indicates a compiler bug that must be fixed before shipping, with no room for numerical tolerance.
Differential testing eliminates the need for golden tests entirely because random inputs provide statistically stronger coverage than any fixed input set.

explanation: A: differential testing shines at corner-case discovery via random input generation. B: reproducibility of failures requires input recording (seeds, tensor state) — this is the hallmark of usable differential testing. C is wrong: compiler transformations legitimately reorder floating-point ops and produce numerically different (though within tolerance) outputs; discrepancy in low-order bits is expected. D is wrong: golden tests remain useful for regression on known-hard inputs and for reproducibility.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard scope and value proposition.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: eager vs compiled comparisons expect tolerance, not bit equality.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: golden and differential tests are complementary.

assumptions: The two implementations are actually independent, not two builds of the same code path.
nonImplications: Does not imply differential testing catches all bugs; some bugs are input-distribution-dependent.
Does not imply golden tests are obsolete; they cover named regressions and reproducibility.
